headline: Deported by mistake in 2025. He flew to Spain on his own.
summary: Kilmar Ábrego García landed in Spain on Wednesday. The Trump administration deported him to El Salvador in March 2025, admitted the error, and brought him back to face trafficking charges a judge later threw out. Then it tried Uganda, Ghana or Liberia. He chose Spain instead. Senator Chris Van Hollen called him "a free man."

cover_question.q: Can you be sent away by mistake?

cover_answer: He was. The government admitted it, and judges stepped in.
table_question: If someone wrongs you and admits it, what do they owe you?

5-7.script: A man named Kilmar lived in Maryland. Last year the government put him on a plane to the country he was born in, then said it was a mistake, like a package mailed to the wrong house. Judges made them bring him back. This week he picked a new country, Spain, and a senator says he is safe there.
5-7.why: The wrong-house package is the whole mistake. The ending is his to choose.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reads a parent's face before the words, so the script gives one picture: a package mailed to the wrong house. The prison and the gang stay out; a child this age can do nothing with them. Expect 'could that happen to us?' Not to you. The fight was about a man who came here without papers as a teenager.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In 2019 a judge ruled it unsafe to send Kilmar Ábrego García to El Salvador. In 2025 the government sent him there anyway, and the Supreme Court made it bring him back. It tried Uganda, Ghana and Liberia; a judge blocked that. A rule only counts if the referee enforces it. Here the referees were judges.
8-12.why: Order, broken order, court, new country. Judges are the referee.
8-12.why_long: An eleven-year-old is testing whether adults follow their rules, and here a government broke a judge's order and was told to fix it. The script walks the chain, 2019 ruling to 2025 flight to Supreme Court, judges as referee. Expect 'did he do anything wrong?' He came without papers as a teenager. The charges were dropped.

13-17.script: If the government deports a man by mistake, what does it owe him? The US sent Kilmar Ábrego García to a Salvadoran prison in 2025, brought him back under court order, charged him and lost. He left for Spain himself this week. Second: is leaving on your own terms a win, or did the pressure work?
13-17.why: Two true things: the courts held, and he still left the country.
13-17.why_long: A fourteen-year-old can hold two true things, and the script hands over both: the courts stopped every attempt to send him where he did not choose, and he is still gone. Then the harder one: is a voluntary exit after eighteen months of pressure voluntary? Expect 'so who won?' I don't know. He is in Spain, not Maryland.

5-7.q: Can you be sent away by mistake?
5-7.a: He was. The government said so, and judges made them bring him back.

8-12.q: Why did he go to Spain?
8-12.a: He chose it. The government wanted Uganda, Ghana or Liberia.
A judge said El Salvador was unsafe. They sent him there anyway.

13-17.q: What does the government owe him?
13-17.a: The courts said bring him back. The articles don't say he got more.

13-17.q: Is leaving on your own terms a win?
13-17.a: Van Hollen calls him "a free man." He also had to leave Maryland.
